summary: "Shanghai Jiao Tong and StepFun built a native macOS sandbox where coding agents' commands migrate between Macs — four Mac mini M4 nodes deliver 1.68–2.05x command throughput and cut tool waiting by 18.8%."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-13-metal-sandbox-apple-silicon-gpu-coding-agents.svg"

Training and evaluating models that generate Apple Metal kernels has a scheduling problem, not a modeling one. A single agent session alternates between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution — so the GPU sits idle for most of the rollout, and running several sessions at once on one Mac just makes them fight over the same accelerator. **Metal Sandbox**, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the Beijing Zhongguancun Academy and StepFun, attacks the idle time directly: native macOS toolchains, per-instance filesystem isolation, and a command-level scheduler that spreads work across interconnected Macs.

**The execution model is deliberately concrete.** Each agent instance owns a workspace and a private development environment on its *owner* node; the node actually running a given command is its *execution* node. Parallel commands run concurrently, serial commands share one execution slot per node, and eligible waiting commands **migrate** to a free Mac — with the source node holding the command and the target returning the result to the original agent. The integration with **Harbor** gives task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection in one workflow, and supports Claude Code, Codex, and mini-SWE-agent.

**The measured gains are meaningful on modest hardware.** Four Mac mini M4 nodes delivered **1.68×–2.05× command throughput** gains under concentrated demand. Replaying **sixteen measured agent traces** under dynamic scheduling put the sustained-throughput gain at **2.14×** for four sessions per node versus one, cut **mean tool waiting by 18.8%**, and shortened **batch elapsed time by 22.3%**.

**The authors are careful about the caveat that matters.** The sustained-throughput figure assumes continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean phase durations; replayed traces cannot capture how different tool feedback changes agent behavior or kernel quality. And the per-trajectory distribution is symmetric — eight trajectories accumulated less tool waiting and eight more — so the headline averages hide that spread. This is scheduling infrastructure for a workload (local Metal kernel search) that is currently a corner of the field; the interesting part is that the same pattern — command-level migration across heterogeneous nodes — is exactly what GPU-cluster agent frameworks need.

The infrastructure and its Harbor integration are open source on GitHub.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.17294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17294)
